summary:
## Shannel's Medusa Look: Key Concepts

This document outlines the key techniques Shannel uses to create her iconic Medusa look from RuPaul's Drag Race Season 1.

### Eyebrow Blocking

For a durable base, Shannel blocks her eyebrows using a strong adhesive.

*   **Product Choice**: Shannel uses **prosthetic adhesive** rather than a glue stick.
*   **Application**: Apply a heavy amount of adhesive, pushing the brow hairs upwards to fully saturate them. Wipe excess from the edges with a wet cloth.
*   **Drying & Setting**: Dry completely with a hairdryer on a cool setting. Once dry, press a generous amount of setting powder over the brow to seal the adhesive.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Prosthetic adhesive provides a stronger, more sweat-resistant hold that is less likely to crack or pull apart during a performance, making it ideal for stage artists.

### Foundation & Base Application

Creating a multi-dimensional and flawless canvas is crucial. Shannel uses several shades of a heavy, low-oil foundation stick.

*   **Covering Brows**: Pat foundation over the powdered-down brows with a finger to create a seamless surface.
*   **Color Placement**: Apply **three different foundation shades** for natural contouring.
    *   **Lightest Shade**: Apply to the center of the face (forehead, down the nose, upper lip, chin).
    *   **Medium Shade**: Used as the main base color.
    *   **Darkest Shade**: Apply to the outer perimeter of the face (hairline, jaw).
*   **Blending**: Use a damp **Beauty Blender** to stipple and blend the foundation shades together for a smooth gradient.

### Contouring for Dimension

Shannel uses a two-step process involving both cream and powder products to sculpt the face.

1.  **Cream Contour**: Before powdering the full face, use a significantly darker foundation stick to draw hard contour lines.
    *   **Cheekbones**: Draw a line from the top of the ear towards the corner of the mouth.
    *   **Jawline**: Apply under the chin and along the jaw to create definition.
    *   **Nose**: Draw two parallel lines down the sides of the nose, creating a 'V' shape at the tip for a slimming effect.
2.  **Powder Contour & Blush**:
    *   After a light powder set, use a **non-shimmer powder bronzer** over the cream contour lines, keeping the color darkest at the hairline and fading it inward.
    *   Apply a **bright pink or orange blush** by patting it onto the apples of the cheeks.
3.  **Baking**:
    *   Apply a thick layer of **translucent powder** under the cheekbone contour line to create a sharp, clean edge. This is brushed away later.
    *   Apply a **bright white eyeshadow** down the center bridge of the nose to highlight.

### Burgundy Smokey Eye

A smokey eye is about the technique of blending, not just the color black.

*   **Base Color**: Use a flat brush to smudge a **deep burgundy eyeshadow** all over the eyelid and slightly into the crease.
*   **Blending Color**: Use a **rusty-orange eyeshadow** to blend the edges of the burgundy upwards and outwards towards the hairline.
*   **Intensifying**: Pat **black eyeshadow** into the outer corner of the eye to add depth and intensity.

### Eyeliner & Lashes

Dramatic eyeliner and lashes frame the eye look.

*   **Top Liner**: Use a **black cake eyeliner** activated with water and a small brush. Draw the line significantly above the natural lash line for a bigger, more dramatic eye shape, extending into a wing and a sharp inner corner.
*   **Bottom Liner**: Line the entire **waterline** with a soft, black pencil. Smudge the burgundy and rust eyeshadows along the lower lash line to connect the top and bottom.
*   **Lashes**: Curl natural lashes, apply mascara, and then apply a dramatic **false lash strip**. Place the strip *above* the natural lash line, nestled into the exaggerated eyeliner, and conceal the band with another layer of cake liner.

### Lips & Finishing Touches

Shannel creates a full, vibrant lip without using any traditional lipstick.

> [!TIP]
> Shannel exclusively uses **eyeshadows** to create her lip color, which provides a matte, highly pigmented finish.

*   **Overdrawing**: Use a lip pencil to draw the desired shape, overdrawing to create a fuller lip. Create a prominent cupid's bow and a rounded bottom lip.
*   **Coloring**: Feather the lip pencil inward, then use a wet, angled brush to line and fill the lips with **burgundy and rust eyeshadows**, mimicking the colors used on the eyes. Finish with a clear lip stain or gloss.
transcription:
## Introduction: Recreating the Medusa Look

Hey guys, it's Shannel from season 1 of Drag Race and we've got all of our makeup set up here and we are ready to go. We're going to recreate the Medusa look from season 1 with the boobs and the headdress that fell off and all that crazy stuff. So it's going to be an amazing, amazing time today. We're going to have a lot of fun and we're going to learn some things. And so I'm going to take you from this to this.

## Blocking Eyebrows with Prosthetic Adhesive

Alright, so we are ready to go. I got my headband on and everything is situated. The first part of my process always is to cover my eyebrows. A lot of queens use a glue stick, which is awesome. I used to use it myself. However, I find that when I sweat a lot it tends to crack or to pull apart. So I use a prosthetic adhesive and I feel like it's a little bit stronger. It kind of has a consistency of like an Elmer's Glue. 

So what I want to do is I want to go ahead and dip into there and I put a heavy amount of it on the brow. And I kind of want to push the brow in an upward position, getting all of that glue as much as you possibly can inside the hairs. I then take a washcloth that's wet and I wipe off all of the edges, top and the bottom to it, top and bottom. And take a hair dryer on cool.

Wipe off the extra edges of the glue. And again, it's kind of a tricky product, but when you kind of master it, it does make a difference. Glue is a little easier but if you're someone that sweats a lot, like myself, this kind of tends to be a little bit of an easier product to avoid all of that. Before I do the other side, I'm going to take a powder puff with my darker powder, because I always use two different powders, and I want to powder over it just to make sure that you really sealed in all of that glue really, really well. And start working on the other brow.

## Applying a Multi-Shade Foundation Base

All right, so now that we got the brows glued down and powdered, I want to put my foundation over them. And instead of rolling foundation on, I like to use my finger with the foundation. I use a foundation stick because I like to use the finger to get in there. Oh yeah, using a finger to get in there sometimes is a really good thing, isn't it? We're going to put the foundation on over the brow to get it covered and then we're going to start to build all of the rest of the foundation on the rest of our face.

You want to use a really good heavy-based foundation, preferably with a minimal amount of mineral oil so you don't end up getting like all greasy and nasty, especially if you're a stage performer and you're performing all the time. Then you want to pick up your Beauty Blender which is your best friend in the entire world and literally start building your color. I use three different shades of foundation, so I start with the upper part of the face and the center parts of your face. So down the center of your nose, forehead, cheeks, upper lip and chin are the lightest parts of your face. The darkest parts of your face are on the outside, so you want to use your darker foundation color towards the outermost parts of your face and then keep everything light in the center. 

Then we're going to pick up the lighter color with our other Beauty Blender. Like ghostly white, literally, it's horrible. The foundation colors I use are nowhere near what my natural skin tone is, which is okay, because when you apply your powders, because I use two different powders, a lighter and a darker powder, it tends to warm it up and become more of what your natural, you know, skin tone essentially should be per se. Cover all these lines in my forehead. God, I need some Botox. Get some of my darker color again. And obviously I'm ghetto here, I'm running out of my color, so I'm scraping it out with the end of a makeup brush. Just so gross. Don't be of hurried to pile that color on. No, really, really, really get it in there.

## Cream Contouring for Definition

I'm gonna pick up my lighter color again for the chin. Now, because you're using different foundations, you see lines obviously where the foundation colors kind of collide. So you can lightly take your Beauty Blender and stipple them kind of together a little bit to blend them out a little bit more. Now, because I don't have obviously any definition for cheekbones at all, I have to basically create it. And so again, before using my contours and my powders to do it, I go in with an even significantly darker foundation and I start to create hard lines around the temples. 

Because again, remember the outsides of our face are our darker areas. So we want to apply that color and get that color in with all the depth towards the outside first. And then under the chin, because God knows I would like one chin instead of three. And then the nose. I naturally have a bump in my nose and the tip of my nose is thick and I don't, I don't like it so I want a stupid thin nose. Using the edges here, we're going to do lines down and I do them kind of into a V sort of motion. Now I go back in and I lightly want to kind of feather this darker color now in with the lighter color.

## Powder Contouring, Blush, and Baking

All right, and now I am ready to put some powder on. Powder a little bit on my upper lip first. My darker powder and my lighter powder on just the lighter areas of the skin. Now we're going to start to actually contour. So I'm going to grab my angle brush and I'm going to grab my non-shimmer bronzers. And now because of where I put that line I can actually start to build the color right over the top of it. And you always typically want to have your color darkest towards the hairline or where your Sideburn area would be and then you want it to fade into going into softer, towards the apple of the cheek. And I always like to keep a towel on my lap, because whenever I pick up my color I always like to kind of brush it off or wipe it off a little bit on the towel before I actually apply it to the skin. 

However much contour you put on is really just truly dependent on how severe a look you like or how soft a look that you like. I guess I kind of go with something a little in between, I don't know, I've gone through different stages. Take a larger brush and then really just kind of pull that color down. And then I like to take like a baby pink and an orange, kind of feather them into the bronzer color a little bit. And pick up my translucent powder again and do this kind of imaginary line that will later be brushed away.

Now we're going to contour the nose. And I like to use, actually it's a paintbrush to be honest with you, but it's just very flat, it's not synthetic hair, it's real hair. And using the same contour type color, I go in from that same line that I created earlier all the way down the nose and into the corner of the eye here where the brow area was. And then I take my bright white shadow, this little painter's sponge thing, literally bright white right down the center of the nose. And again, just going to let it sit there and kind of milk for just a little bit. And then I like to take a large brush, it's actually very flat here, for my blush and I like to use like a bright kind of a color. And you just want to pat it in the apple of the cheek. You don't have to scrub that color on and like get crazy with that. I see a lot of queens and they're just like, you know, from freaking one end of their face to the other with the blush, which I mean, it's fine, but sometimes it can just be a lot.

## Creating a Burgundy Smokey Eye

Okay, so we have finished the foundation, the powder and the contour and now we're going to move on to the eyes. I love to do a smokey eye. I think because having light eyes, I like to have a lot of dark color around my eyes, be it blacks, burgundies, purples, fuchsia, whatever the colors are. And so on the Medusa episode, I happen to do a smokey eye. 

I like to take a brush that obviously has been completely mutilated at this point, but it's real fiber and I think it's squirrel hair or something like that, I don't know, but it's really flat. And so I like to go with a very deep burgundy tone to begin with. And basically what I do is I just take and I start literally just kind of smudging it all over the actual lid of the eye up into the crease just a little bit. So this is this deep burgundy tone all over the lid, kind of smudged up into the crease.

Doing a smokey eye also doesn't necessarily mean it has to be like black or brown or gray or whatever. Smokey eye basically just means that you're using a color all over the lid up through, you know, into the crease area of the eye. I think a lot of times people get confused by when they hear smokey eye and they assume well that means it has to be black, and it doesn't. 

So now that I've got the burgundy all over, I'm going to use this kind of an orangey rust color and that becomes kind of my blending color. So I smudge it in with the purple, the burgundy purple, and I pull that color up even further and then taking and sweeping out towards the hairline. So yeah, this kind of this orangey color just helps to blend the burgundies. And again, as you can see, I'm taking and I'm pushing that color out, keeping it darker towards the most innermost parts of the eye through here. And then I want to take and pull my black in in the corners so that I can really intensify the corner most part of the eye. And literally I just take and I start patting this color, this black, in the corner most part of the eye area here. So if you're going to use multiple colors, make sure that when you're applying them and you're putting them on, there's kind of a rhyme and a reason where you're putting it. There's no, you know, science to makeup in the aspect of what's right and what's wrong. I think it's all on a personal and individual level as far as what works for you.

## Applying Eyeliner for a Dramatic Look

Now I'm going to put my eyeliner on. And I like to use like a cream or a cake eyeliner on the uppermost part of the eye and a pencil on the bottom. I want to go in with my cake liner with a fairly small brush, it almost looks like a lip brush actually, and I use water. So I'm going to start from the innermost part of the eye, pulling that black all the way. And I don't even use my actual lash line as a guide, I bring it up significantly farther. And then I always bring it in in the corner most part of my eye here as well and then you connect it at the bottom part of the eye. 

Okay, so now that I got the cake eyeliner on the top, I'm going to use like the blackest black pencil on the whole waterline of the bottom part of the eye. And literally you have to like open your mouth when you do this and look a fool. It's crazy because nobody ever like really taught me how to do makeup. I think I've always just kind of been an artist and I remember when I got in makeup for the very first time was 15 years old. It was for Halloween and you know using my Mom's makeup and her sponge tip applicators, it was so bad. You really really get a lot of that black around there. Especially for someone who has light eyes like myself, the more black that you put around your eyes, the more intensified they become.

I now am going to go back with this really tiny little brush with that same burgundy I used on my lid and I actually smudge it right into that black. And now I pick up a smaller little angle brush with that rusty orange color and I'm going to smudge it as well into the bottom of the eye. You have to be careful depending upon the shape of the eye that you have because sometimes for certain people who have like a deep set eye, if you apply too much deep color in the innermost part of the eye, in through here, it can actually make your eyes look even further set back. For me, because I have a lot of space there and I don't have a deep set crease, I can tend to put a little bit more color there.

## Crafting the Perfect Vintage Eyebrow

Now we're going to do the eyebrows. And I love a brow. I like a vintage looking brow. And so I like to use again another paint brush, it's this very, very small like angled brush. I don't know what it would be used for in painting but I really like it. And I use a mixture of my spit and water and I use eyeshadow again, and I use like brown burgundy kind of a black mixture with it. 

The shape of your brow is really dependent on what you like—how high, how low, how thick. This is just the undermost part of the line to start with. So before I finish the rest of the brow, I'm going to take and apply a little color underneath the brow. You can use like a white or a nude. Now I'm going to fill in the top part, the top part of the eyebrow, and then kind of picking up a little bit of brown in there as well.

## Applying False Lashes

So we pretty much have the eyes, the brows done, all the stuff. Now is to put on the lashes. So what I always like to do is I like to curl my lashes first and put mascara on my own lashes. 

Okay, so I've taken my lashes and I've put the lash glue on. And as the lash glue is on, I blow on the lash and I round it out. I always start with the outside of the eye and work in towards the corner most part. And again, I'm not even putting them on my actual lash line, but kind of just like in between the liner. And then I will go back with my cake liner that I used on the top part of the eye and I'm just going to put a little bit more of that black liner on the top to get rid of the look of the glue line and to make sure that there's no powder at all. Bam, eyes are done.

## Creating an Overdrawn Lip with Eyeshadow

Now we're going to move on to lips. For me, I always like a bright color, like a reddish or magenta. Nude colors just, they don't look right on me. They look amazing on a lot of Queens, they don't look right on me. But I have a small lip, sadly, so my goal always is to make the lip look as full as I can without it looking ridiculous. 

I actually like to create a half circle and I overdraw the bottom as well. So then I take with the pencil and I like to feather the color in. I don't color in the whole lip but I feather it in to soften the line. And then what I do is I actually go back with another angle brush, kind of like the brow brush basically, and I wet my burgundy eyeshadow and I go over that lip line again. 

Now I actually take my eyeshadow, that rust color, I go right over it. I don't own a tube of lipstick, I use all eyeshadows. And I'm going to put a lip stain over this and the lip is done.

## The Final Look & Outro

And now all I have left to do is to dust off the rest of the powder, maybe put a little more contour, a little more blush back on. So guys, this was the season 1 Medusa look Runway and I hope you guys enjoyed it. I hope you learned something and you can take some of that knowledge home and apply it to your own face. 

Hey squirrel friend, when one video ends, just open up another one. It's called binge viewing. Go ahead, I support you.
